1226.title: Islamic finance
1226.hook: partnership, profit-sharing and leasing as alternatives
1226.howItsDone: Islamic banks and community lenders offer home financing, savings and business funding through partnership, profit-sharing, leasing and cost-plus sale contracts, with boards of scholars reviewing the products.

segments.voice: Yesterday, riba, and your line: no interest. Trade permitted, riba forbidden, and the question of who carries the risk.

If lending money for a fixed return is off the table, how does anyone start a business, buy a house, or grow savings? Muslim jurists asked that too. Their answer starts with a picture older than the loan. One person has money and no time; another has skill and no money. They agree: you take my capital and trade with it, and whatever profit comes, we split as we agreed today. If the caravan comes home rich, both are glad. If it is lost, both lose.
screen: `NO LOAN FOR A FIXED RETURN. THEN WHAT?` → `MONEY MEETS SKILL.` → `BOTH WIN OR BOTH LOSE.`

segments.voice: The fiqh books describe several contracts that move money without riba. Four are worth knowing. First, mudarabah, the picture from the hook: one side brings capital, the other brings work, profit is shared by an agreed ratio, and if money is lost, the investor bears that loss while the worker loses the effort. Second, musharakah, a full partnership: both put in capital and share profit and loss together. Some home-financing plans use a version of it, where the buyer and the bank own the house together and the buyer slowly buys out the bank's part. Third, ijarah, leasing: the owner rents out a car, a machine, a building, and earns rent for its use while still owning it, with the risks ownership brings. Fourth, murabaha, a sale at cost plus a stated profit: the seller buys the goods first and sells them on, sometimes with payment later. Behind all four sits a principle from a report in Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi: gain goes with liability. Whoever takes the profit must also be exposed to the loss. That's the difference the scholars see between rent and interest, or between a partner's share and a lender's fee. And they argue about it honestly. Some scholars and economists have criticized products that, in their view, follow the letter but look a lot like a loan with a new name; others defend them as lawful steps along the way. The ideal both sides point to is the same: share the risk.
screen: `MUDARABAH: MONEY MEETS WORK.` · `MUSHARAKAH: PARTNERS IN PROFIT AND LOSS.` · `IJARAH AND MURABAHA: LEASE AND SALE.` · `GAIN GOES WITH LIABILITY.`

If it slips, go back to the picture: the one with money, the one with skill, and the caravan that might or might not come home.
Islamic finance. Contracts like partnership, profit-sharing, leasing and cost-plus sale, built so that the one who gains also carries risk. Today's word.
Your line: share the risk. Whoever takes the gain stands under the loss too. Rest well.

1227.title: Clear contracts
1227.howItsDone: Islamic law asks that contracts be clear, freely agreed and free of excessive uncertainty, and the Qur'an asks that debts with a term be written down with witnesses; Muslim scholars review modern contracts with these conditions in mind.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Islamic finance, and your line: share the risk. Money meets skill, and both win or both lose.

Spring in an orchard. The date palms have just set their fruit, small and green, nowhere near ready. A buyer walks up and offers the farmer a price for the whole crop, right now. The farmer could use the cash; the buyer is gambling on a good harvest. Both are adults, both willing. And yet the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, in a report in Sahih al-Bukhari, forbade selling fruit before its ripening shows. Why stop a deal two people want?
screen: `GREEN FRUIT ON THE PALM.` → `A PRICE FOR THE WHOLE CROP.` → `NOT YET, SAYS THE PROPHET.`

segments.voice: Day three hundred eighty-eight met the verse that opens surah five, in Pickthall's words: "O ye who believe! Fulfil your undertakings." The word he renders undertakings is 'uqud, the plural of 'aqd, a contract. Since it's addressed to believers, keeping a contract becomes part of faith, not just good business. Today, what the jurists said makes a contract real enough to keep. Three answers. First, clarity. Near the end of surah two, believers who contract a debt for a fixed term are told to write it down, with a scribe who writes fairly, and witnesses. Paper, so memory can't bend it later. Second, consent. The Qur'an speaks of trade by mutual agreement, and the jurists hold that a contract made under pressure or trickery doesn't bind the way a free one does. Third, no excessive uncertainty, called gharar. In Sahih Muslim, the Prophet forbids the sale decided by a thrown pebble and the sale of gharar. That's the orchard: unripe fruit might become a harvest or nothing, and one side pays for a gamble neither can see. Excessive, the scholars say, because ordinary deals carry a little uncertainty; you can't know the exact taste of a melon. What's forbidden is the kind that turns a sale into a bet. Clear words, a free yes, and enough knowledge on both sides: an 'aqd worth keeping.
screen: `'AQD: KEEP YOUR CONTRACTS.` · `CLARITY: WRITE IT DOWN.` · `CONSENT: A FREE YES.` · `NO GHARAR: NOT A GAMBLE.`

segments.voice: Think of something you agreed to lately without really reading it: an app's terms, a lease, a vague promise to a friend. Ask today's three questions: is it clear what each side gives, was the yes free, is something hidden that neither side could see? You don't need answers; just notice which of the three is shakiest, and let it rest with your breathing.
'Aqd. A contract, which the Qur'an tells believers to fulfill, made with clear terms, free consent and no excessive uncertainty. Today's word.
Your line: clear terms. Tomorrow, the creatures who can't sign anything at all. Go gently, and see you then.

1228.title: Animals' rights
1228.hook: don't overload, don't brand faces, don't make them targets (Muslim)
1228.howItsDone: Islamic law requires owners to feed and rest their animals and not to overwork them, and forbids striking or branding their faces and using living creatures as targets.

segments.voice: Yesterday, 'aqd, the contract, and your line: clear terms. Clear words, a free yes, and no gamble hidden inside.

Tears, running from a camel's eyes. That's where a report in Abu Dawud begins, in a walled garden in Medina belonging to a man of the Ansar. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ steps inside, and the camel tied there sees him and begins to groan. He strokes it behind the ears until it settles, then asks: whose camel is this? A young man comes running. And the Prophet tells him to fear God about this animal, because it has complained that its owner starves it and wears it out.
screen: `A CAMEL IN A WALLED GARDEN.` → `IT GROANS, THEN SETTLES.` → `IT COMPLAINED OF YOU.`

segments.voice: Day two hundred seventy-two gave us the man who carried water up a well for a thirsty dog. Today, the law's side. The Qur'an sets the frame. In surah six, every creature on the earth and every bird that flies on two wings are communities like you, and they too will be gathered to their Lord. Communities, not furniture. From that the fiqh books draw duties, and today's three come from the hadith. First, don't overload. Another report in Abu Dawud tells of the Prophet passing a camel so thin its back had nearly reached its belly: fear God about these animals that cannot speak; ride them while they are fit, and eat of them while they are fit. The jurists made it a rule: an owner must feed an animal and may not work it beyond its strength. Second, don't brand or strike faces. In Sahih Muslim, the Prophet forbids hitting the face and branding the face, and when he passes a donkey branded on its face, he curses whoever did it. Third, don't make them targets. Also in Sahih Muslim, Ibn Umar comes across young men shooting at a bird they've tied up. They scatter, and he tells them the Prophet cursed anyone who makes a living thing a target. So the fiqh books speak of an animal's rights the way they speak of a neighbor's: food, rest, a fair load, a face left unbranded. A camel can't file a complaint. The tradition says it filed one anyway, and the Prophet heard it.
screen: `COMMUNITIES LIKE YOU.` · `DON'T OVERLOAD: FEED AND REST THEM.` · `DON'T BRAND OR STRIKE THE FACE.` · `DON'T MAKE THEM TARGETS.`

segments.voice: If there's a pet near you, check its water and sit with it a while. If not, bring to mind an animal you see often, a neighbor's dog, a bird on the wire, and ask what it needs that only a person can give: food, water, shade, a lighter load. Hold it kindly, and if you pray, you can remember it there.
Animals' rights. In Islamic law, what an animal is owed: food, rest, a fair load, a face left unharmed, and never to be used as a target. Today's word.
Your line: they have rights. Even the ones who can't speak for themselves. I'll be here tomorrow.

1229.title: Medical questions
1229.hook: modern fiqh on transplants, IVF, end of life, where scholars reason and differ
1229.howItsDone: Muslim patients and families facing questions about transplants, fertility treatment or end-of-life care may ask a trusted scholar or consult the rulings of fiqh councils, which reason from the Qur'an, the hadith and the purposes of the law.

segments.voice: Yesterday, animals' rights, and your line: they have rights. A camel complained in a garden, and the Prophet heard it.

Brain-dead. A doctor says the word to a family in a hospital corridor late at night, about their father, and gently asks about donating his kidneys. A few floors up, a young couple is talking with a fertility clinic. At the end of the hall, a grandmother's machines keep her body going after her doctors say they can no longer help. None of this is in the Qur'an by name. The jurists of Baghdad and Cordoba never saw a ventilator. Yet a Muslim family in that corridor might call a scholar and ask: what does the law say?
screen: `A HOSPITAL CORRIDOR AT NIGHT.` → `DONATION, FERTILITY, MACHINES.` → `NONE OF IT NAMED IN THE TEXT.`

segments.voice: Start with medicine itself. In Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ says that God has not sent down a disease without also sending down its cure. Seeking treatment is part of the tradition. Then the method. Scholars look for a text that speaks to the new question, reason by analogy from cases that do appear, and weigh the purposes of the law, which we'll meet in two days. That effort is called ijtihad. Organ transplants: some fiqh councils have allowed donation, within limits, reading it through the verse in surah five that whoever saves a life, it is as if he had saved all of humankind. Other scholars have objected, out of reverence for the body after death, which the tradition protects. Fertility: Sunni councils have allowed IVF between a married couple, using their own egg and sperm, and refused a third party's; some Shia authorities have reasoned more widely, allowing some forms of donation. Same texts, different reasoning, both careful. End of life: the same verse likens killing one soul to killing all humankind, and scholars read it as forbidding a deliberately ended life. Some allow stopping treatment that only prolongs dying, when doctors judge there is no hope of recovery, and brain death is still argued. So the answer is often not one fatwa but a few, each showing its reasoning. That isn't confusion. It's an old method, honestly applied.
screen: `GOD SENT A CURE WITH EVERY DISEASE.` · `IJTIHAD: TEXT, ANALOGY, PURPOSE.` · `TRANSPLANTS AND IVF: COUNCILS DIFFER.` · `END OF LIFE: NO KILLING, SOME LETTING GO.`

segments.voice: Think of one medical decision someone you love has faced, or might, and name it plainly: donation, a treatment, a hard ending. Ask today's three questions gently: is there a text, is there a case like it, what is the law trying to protect? Then hold the person and the question side by side. If a hard ending is close for you, or you're thinking of ending your own life, call or text 988 in the US, or your local emergency number.

1230.title: Law and mercy
1230.hook: the law is meant to bring ease: Allah wants ease for you (2:185)
1230.howItsDone: Muslims who are traveling, ill or unable to keep a rule in full use the permissions the law gives, such as shortening prayers, making up fasts later, praying seated, or wiping with clean earth when water can't be used.

segments.voice: Yesterday, medical questions, and your line: old method, new questions. Text, then analogy, then purpose, for cases nobody could have imagined.

A Bedouin man is urinating on the floor of the mosque in Medina, and the companions are already on their feet, shouting at him. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ tells them to leave him alone. Let him finish, then pour a bucket of water over the spot. And, in the report in Sahih al-Bukhari, he tells them they were sent to make things easy, not hard. Afterward he speaks gently to the man about what a mosque is for. A floor can be washed. A person driven away is harder to bring back.
screen: `A BEDOUIN IN THE MOSQUE.` → `THE COMPANIONS LEAP UP.` → `LEAVE HIM. POUR WATER.`

segments.voice: The key line sits in the fasting verses of surah two. Right after allowing the sick and the traveler to make up their fast on other days, the Qur'an says, in Pickthall's words: "Allah desireth for you ease; He desireth not hardship for you." Not in a poem about mercy, but in the middle of a rule. The ease is part of the law, not an exception to it. The jurists built on this. A traveler may shorten the prayers. Someone without water, or too ill to use it, may wipe with clean earth instead of washing, a practice called tayammum. In Sahih al-Bukhari, a man with an illness asks how to pray, and the Prophet tells him: stand, and if you can't, sit, and if you can't, lie on your side. Each step down is still prayer. These easings are called rukhsah, a permission, and a report in Musnad Ahmad says God loves His permissions to be taken. Aisha reports, also in Bukhari, that whenever the Prophet was given a choice between two matters he chose the easier, as long as it was not a sin. That last clause matters: ease isn't anything goes, and the law still has edges. Inside them, the default is mercy, and scholars made it a maxim: hardship brings ease. So a teacher who makes the law heavier than it is can be corrected from inside the tradition itself.
screen: `EASE, IN THE MIDDLE OF A RULE.` · `SHORTEN, WIPE, SIT, LIE DOWN.` · `HE CHOSE THE EASIER, IF NOT A SIN.` · `HARDSHIP BRINGS EASE.`

segments.voice: Find one place where you've made something harder than it needs to be: a rule you keep for yourself, a standard you hold a friend to, a habit at work that only adds weight. Ask whether the hard way is required or just habit, and if an easier way crosses no line, picture choosing it and notice your shoulders. If you pray, you can remember the verse about ease.
Law and mercy. In Islam, the law itself carries ease: permissions for the sick, the traveler and the weak, and a preference for the easier path where no sin is involved. Today's word.
Your line: ease, not hardship. The bucket of water comes before the shouting. Until tomorrow.

1231.title: The spirit of the law
1231.hook: the rules serve the aims: life, mind, faith, family, property
1231.howItsDone: Muslim scholars use the maqasid al-shari'ah, the aims of the law, to explain existing rules and to guide reasoning on new questions, while holding that the aims serve the texts rather than replace them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, law and mercy, and your line: ease, not hardship. A floor washed with a bucket of water, and a man not driven away.

Can a starving man eat what the law forbids? Say a traveler is lost in the desert, days without food, and the only thing in reach is meat he may not eat. Does he starve with clean hands? The Qur'an has already answered, in surah two, right after listing what is forbidden. In Pickthall's words: "But he who is driven by necessity, neither craving nor transgressing, it is no sin for him." The rule bends because it was there to serve something, and here that something is his life.
screen: `DAYS WITHOUT FOOD.` → `ONLY FORBIDDEN MEAT IN REACH.` → `NO SIN, DRIVEN BY NECESSITY.`

segments.voice: Muslim jurists gave this a name: the maqasid al-shari'ah, the aims of the law. Al-Ghazali, in his book on legal theory, al-Mustasfa, says the law protects five things: religion, life, mind, lineage and property. Later, the Andalusian scholar al-Shatibi built a whole study around these aims. Take each one and a rule comes into focus. Faith: the law protects worship and forbids forcing it; the Qur'an says there is no compulsion in religion. Life: the ban on killing, and the starving traveler's permission. Mind: the ban on wine and other intoxicants, which cloud judgment. Family, or lineage: marriage, the rights of children, the bride's gift. Property: the honest merchant, the clear contract, the ban on riba, the fixed shares of inheritance. Seen this way, the rules of the last two weeks look less like a list and more like a house, every room built to protect something. Scholars use the aims two ways. When texts are clear, the aims explain them. When a new case arrives with no text, like the hospital corridor, the aims guide the reasoning. They also warn against the opposite mistake: using the aims to throw out clear rules whenever they feel inconvenient. The aims serve the texts; they don't replace them. But asking what a rule is for, the jurists say, isn't disrespect. It's how they read.
screen: `DRIVEN BY NECESSITY, NO SIN.` · `AL-GHAZALI: FIVE THINGS PROTECTED.` · `FAITH, LIFE, MIND, FAMILY, PROPERTY.` · `THE AIMS SERVE THE TEXTS.`

segments.voice: Pick one rule from the last two weeks, the wet grain on top, the third by will, the camel's fair load, and ask which of the five it protects: faith, life, mind, family or property. Then try a rule of your own, no phones at dinner, pay on time, pray at dawn, and notice whether it looks different once you can see what it's guarding.

1232.title: Fiqh close
1232.hook: many schools, many scholars, one book, one sunnah
1232.howItsDone: Muslims follow the rulings of a school of law or a trusted scholar, and when a jurist's name is mentioned a Muslim may add a phrase asking Allah's mercy for them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the spirit of the law, and your line: the aim behind it. Faith, life, mind, family, property.

A shelf, to start. On it sits one Qur'an and a few volumes of hadith. Beside it stands a whole wall: Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i and Hanbali books, Ja'fari, Zaydi and Ibadi books, commentaries on commentaries, rulings on wedding gifts, on contracts, on donkeys carrying too much, on hospital beds. For weeks this path has walked along that wall. Today the walk ends, with one last question: how does one small shelf turn into a wall, and still face the same way?
screen: `ONE SMALL SHELF.` → `ONE LONG WALL.` → `STILL FACING THE SAME WAY?`

segments.voice: Start with the word. Fiqh means understanding. In a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ says that when Allah wants good for someone, He gives that person understanding in the religion, and the verb comes from the same root as fiqh. So the whole wall is people trying to understand. Next, the roads. The jurists started from the same place: the Qur'an first, the sunnah second. Then they reasoned out. Some leaned on the agreement of scholars, some on analogy, some on reason itself, as Ja'fari jurists do, some on the common good or the custom of a place. Different tools, different roads. Then, the difference. The Qur'an gives a direction for disputes: "if ye have a dispute concerning any matter, refer it to Allah and the messenger." The schools all claim that same reference point. And Bukhari records a hadith that explains their patience with each other: a judge who strives and gets it right has two rewards, and one who strives and gets it wrong still has one. Effort in good faith is honored even when it misses. Last, the direction. Stand at the back of a mosque at prayer time. One person folds the hands high, another lets them hang. One says amin aloud, another under the breath. Every row still faces the same point.
screen: `FIQH MEANS UNDERSTANDING.` · `ONE START, MANY ROADS.` · `TWO REWARDS, OR ONE.` · then, large: `EVERY ROW FACES ONE POINT.`

segments.voice: Bring one name to mind, someone who did the slow work of understanding: Abu Hanifa, Malik, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Ja'far al-Sadiq, or someone closer, a teacher, an imam, a grandmother who knew how to pray and showed you. If you pray, you may know the custom of asking Allah's mercy for a scholar when the name comes up; if you don't, simply say thank you, in your own head.
Fiqh close. The end of the block on fiqh, the understanding of the law: one book, one sunnah, many schools working from them. Today's word.
